title: Plotting a Binary Outcome
text:
An outcome that takes only the values 0 and 1 puts every point of a scatterplot on one of two horizontal stripes. Dots on the same stripe overlap wherever the feature takes similar values, so the plot hides how many observations there are. Two plots avoid this: a rug and a pair of histograms.
The examples use the Western Collaborative Group Study, which followed 3154 middle-aged men for coronary heart disease (Rosenman et al. 1975). In data/wcgs.csv, the outcome chd is 1 for a man with an incident case and 0 for a man without one. The feature is his body mass index, bmi. Each plot also shows the line fitted to chd by least squares on bmi.

RPython



wcgs <- readr::read_csv("data/wcgs.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_bmi <- lm(chd ~ bmi, data = wcgs)




import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

wcgs = pd.read_csv("data/wcgs.csv")
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(wcgs["bmi"], wcgs["chd"], 1)
fitted_bmi = intercept + slope * wcgs["bmi"]

title: Plotting a Binary Outcome
text:
0.2 A rug







Example 1 (A rug of the WCGS outcome) A rug draws one tick per observation along an axis. Draw the men with chd \(= 0\) along the bottom edge and the men with chd \(= 1\) along the top edge. Transparent ticks darken where many observations share nearly the same bmi.

RPython



library(ggplot2)
ggplot(wcgs, aes(bmi, chd)) +
  geom_rug(data = subset(wcgs, chd == 0), sides = "b", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_rug(data = subset(wcgs, chd == 1), sides = "t", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted(fit_bmi))) +
  labs(x = "Body mass index (bmi)", y = "Fitted chd")



Fitted line of chd on bmi in the WCGS data, with a rug of the men with chd = 1 along the top and chd = 0 along the bottom.








import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for chd, side in [(0, 0.0), (1, 1.0)]:
    bmi_chd = wcgs.loc[wcgs["chd"] == chd, "bmi"]
    ax.plot(bmi_chd, [side] * len(bmi_chd), "|", color="gray", alpha=0.3)
ax.axhline(0, linestyle="--", color="black")
ax.axhline(1, linestyle="--", color="black")
ax.plot(wcgs["bmi"], fitted_bmi)
ax.set_xlabel("Body mass index (bmi)")
ax.set_ylabel("Fitted chd")
plt.show()



Fitted line of chd on bmi in the WCGS data, with a rug of the men with chd = 1 along the top and chd = 0 along the bottom.

title: Plotting a Binary Outcome
text:
0.3 Two histograms







Example 2 (Two histograms of the WCGS feature) A histogram of bmi for the men with chd \(= 0\) stands on the line \(y = 0\). A histogram for the men with chd \(= 1\) hangs down from the line \(y = 1\). Each histogram is scaled so its tallest bar is \(0.3\) high, because there are far fewer cases than non-cases and the raw counts would hide the smaller group. The heights then show each group’s shape, not how many men it holds.

RPython



breaks <- seq(floor(min(wcgs$bmi)), ceiling(max(wcgs$bmi)), by = 1)
bars <- function(data, chd_value) {
  counts <- hist(data$bmi[data$chd == chd_value], breaks = breaks,
                 plot = FALSE)$counts
  tibble::tibble(xmin = head(breaks, -1), xmax = tail(breaks, -1),
                 height = 0.3 * counts / max(counts))
}
bars0 <- bars(wcgs, 0)
bars1 <- bars(wcgs, 1)
ggplot(wcgs, aes(bmi, chd)) +
  geom_rect(data = bars0,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 0, ymax = height),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_rect(data = bars1,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 1 - height, ymax = 1),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted(fit_bmi))) +
  labs(x = "Body mass index (bmi)", y = "Fitted chd")



The same line, with a histogram of bmi for the men with chd = 0 standing on the line y = 0 and one for the men with chd = 1 hanging from the line y = 1. Each histogram is scaled so its tallest bar is 0.3 high.








breaks = np.arange(np.floor(wcgs["bmi"].min()), np.ceil(wcgs["bmi"].max()) + 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for chd, base, sign in [(0, 0.0, 1), (1, 1.0, -1)]:
    counts, _ = np.histogram(wcgs.loc[wcgs["chd"] == chd, "bmi"], bins=breaks)
    ax.bar(breaks[:-1], sign * 0.3 * counts / counts.max(), width=1,
           bottom=base, align="edge", alpha=0.4)
#> <BarContainer object of 28 artists>
#> <BarContainer object of 28 artists>
ax.plot(wcgs["bmi"], fitted_bmi)
#> [<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x7f77f809e210>]
ax.set_xlabel("Body mass index (bmi)")
#> Text(0.5, 0, 'Body mass index (bmi)')
ax.set_ylabel("Fitted chd")
#> Text(0, 0.5, 'Fitted chd')
plt.show()



The same line, with a histogram of bmi for the men with chd = 0 standing on the line y = 0 and one for the men with chd = 1 hanging from the line y = 1. Each histogram is scaled so its tallest bar is 0.3 high.

title: Choosing Colors
text:
With 10 groups, no tested palette keeps every pair easy to tell apart, and the table does not test 8 or 9 groups. Pair color with shape or line type, so that color is never the only way to tell groups apart. Better still, show fewer groups: combine small groups, or split the figure into panels.
The rcartocolor package’s Safe palette gives up to 12 colors, so it is the fallback when a figure needs more than 7 groups. Its smallest distance is about 5 to 6 at every size in the table, which is below the cutoff, so it is a fallback and not a recommendation. The fxtas package uses it for its biomarker groups.








Nowosad, Jakub. 2025. Colorblindcheck: Check Color Palettes for Problems with Color Vision Deficiency. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=colorblindcheck.


Okabe, Masataka, and Kei Ito. 2008. Color Universal Design (CUD): How to Make Figures and Presentations That Are Friendly to Colorblind People. https://jfly.uni-koeln.de/color/.

title: Choosing Colors
text:
A palette that looks distinct to you can merge for readers with a color vision deficiency. Instead of judging by eye, simulate the common kinds of color vision deficiency and measure how far apart the closest two colors get.
The colorblindcheck package (Nowosad 2025) does this. Its palette_check() function returns the smallest distance between two colors of a palette, under normal vision and under each simulated deficiency. As a rule of thumb, a smallest distance of about 10 or more means every pair is easy to tell apart. This chapter uses that rule of thumb as its cutoff; the package does not define one. Below the cutoff, some pair is hard to tell apart for some readers.







Example 1 (Comparing qualitative palettes) This example computes, for each palette and number of groups, the smallest distance between two colors under the worst of the three simulated deficiencies (deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia). A dash marks a palette that has fewer colors than groups.


Show R code
options(knitr.kable.NA = "-")

# order puts blue and vermillion first and leaves out black and grey
okabe_ito_order <- c(5, 6, 3, 7, 2, 1, 4)
brewer <- function(name) {
  function(n) RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(max(n, 3), name)[seq_len(n)]
}
palettes <- list(
  "Okabe-Ito (ggokabeito)" = function(n) {
    ggokabeito::palette_okabe_ito(order = okabe_ito_order)[seq_len(n)]
  },
  "RColorBrewer Dark2" = brewer("Dark2"),
  "RColorBrewer Set2" = brewer("Set2"),
  "RColorBrewer Paired" = brewer("Paired"),
  "khroma muted" = function(n) unname(khroma::color("muted")(n)),
  "viridis" = function(n) viridisLite::viridis(n),
  "rcartocolor Safe" = function(n) rcartocolor::carto_pal(n, "Safe")
)

worst_case_distance <- function(make_palette, n) {
  colors <- tryCatch(
    make_palette(n),
    error = function(e) NULL,
    warning = function(w) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(colors) || length(colors) < n || anyNA(colors)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  # viridis adds an alpha channel; palette_check() wants plain "#rrggbb"
  colors <- substr(as.character(colors), 1, 7)
  # the first row is normal vision; the rest are the simulated deficiencies
  min(colorblindcheck::palette_check(colors)$min_dist[-1])
}

expand.grid(palette = names(palettes), groups = c(3, 5, 7, 10)) |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    distance = worst_case_distance(palettes[[as.character(palette)]], groups)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = groups,
    values_from = distance,
    names_prefix = "n = "
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)

Example 1 shows the results. The Okabe-Ito palette (Okabe and Ito 2008) stays above 10 for all 7 of its colors, and with 10 groups no palette tested reaches 10. The RColorBrewer qualitative palettes Dark2 and Set2 are fine for 3 groups and then lose distinctness quickly. The viridis palette scores well for 3 and 5 groups, but it is a sequential palette, so its neighboring colors look alike when the groups have no order. The khroma package’s Okabe-Ito scheme starts with black, so it is not comparable here. Its muted scheme has at most 9 colors.
